utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please give us the case number and have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-95-10-PT, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I think there are some photographers in this room. Thank you. I would like the representatives of the Prosecution to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is Tochilovsky, and I appear with my colleague Mr. Bowers for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tochilovsky. Thank you, Mr. Terree Bowers. The representatives for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Veselin Londrovic, Defence counsel for the accused, Goran Jelisic. Mr. Jovan Babic, my colleague from Novi Sad, appears together with me today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Londrovic. Good morning, Mr. Babic. Mr. Jelisic, will you rise please for a moment? Good morning. I believe that your counsel have told you why you are appearing today. Today, for you, you must confirm for the Tribunal what your plea is going to be in the trial which has been brought against you by the Prosecutors of the International Tribunal. You have already appeared once, and further to discussions with the Office of the Prosecutor, yourself, and your counsel, the indictment has been amended. This is further to a Status Conference which was presided over by Judge Riad who was the Judge assigned for that purpose. As we did when you appeared for the first time before the Tribunal, we are going to have another initial appearance. We're going to have the indictment read to you, and then the Judges will note what plea is going to be yours, that is, the choice you've made together with your lawyers. We would like to know whether you plead guilty or not guilty. Do you understand what I've just said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honours. I have understood everything you've said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic? You may be seated, Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on behalf of the Defence and on behalf of the accused, Mr. Jelisic, I ask you kindly to close this session to the public for a short period of time so that we could discuss certain matters from our motion dated the 22nd of October this year. I hope that the Trial Chamber has received this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me check. Mr. Registrar, what is the document that Mr. Londrovic is referring to? The registrar has just told me. This will be a private session, but for the public, I would like to say that the initial appearance is public and it will be public, but in order to present the reasons that you explained in a letter, we will move into a private session for a few moments. Mr. Registrar, would you have the technicians turn this session into a private session? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is a public hearing once again. Mr. Registrar, we're going to ask you to read the entire indictment. Let me point out to Mr. Jelisic and to his counsel that we will not read those charges which deal with the co-accused. I'm not going to give that person's name. It's not important. However, we will focus the reading on those charges which deal only with Mr. Jelisic, and we will listen to his plea of guilty or not guilty. Mr. Jelisic, at the proper time for pleading, I will ask you to rise, and this is not the time to do so, and you will say to us very clearly whether you plead guilty or not guilty. Let me remind you so that things will be clear, the provisions of Rule 62, with which you must be familiar, that the right of the accused to counsel is respected, that we will have the indictment read to the accused in a language that he speaks and understands, and that the accused understands the indictment. This was done during the initial appearance, and you were asked to plead guilty or not guilty to each of the charges. Let me remind you, and I say this to your counsel as well, that if the accused does not plead, then you will be considered as having pleaded not guilty and your rights will be fully respected. In case the question of the plea of guilty comes into play, there is Rule 62 bis that we can refer to, that if the accused pleads guilty or requests that his plea of not guilty be retracted, this must be made voluntary and not be equivocal, and that there are sufficient factual bases for the crime and the accused's participation in it. All of this must have been explained to you in conversations with your counsel. Mr. Registrar, would you now read us the indictment for the Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic? Please, don't forget to turn the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic, Second Amended Indictment, Louise Arbour, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, charges: 1) Beginning on about 30 April, 1992, Serb forces from Bosnia and elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia fought to obtain control of Brcko, a town and municipality in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the former Yugoslavia. Serb forces forcibly expelled Croat and Muslim residents from their homes and, with the assistance of local Serb authorities, held them at collection centres, where many were killed, beaten, and otherwise mistreated. Many of the women, children, and elderly were confined at the nearby village of Brezovo Polje. Most of the men of military age, and a few women, were taken to Luka camp. 2) From about 7 May, 1992 until early July 1992, Serb forces confined hundreds of Muslim and Croat men, and a few women, at Luka camp in inhumane conditions and under armed guard. From about 7 May, 1992 until a about 21 May, 1992, detainees were systematically killed at Luka. Almost every day during that time, the accused, often assisted by camp guards, entered Luka's main hangar where most detainees were kept, selected detainees for interrogation, beat them, and then often shot and killed them. 3) The accused, often assisted the camp guards, usually shot detainees at close range in the head or back. Often, the accused and camp guards forced the detainees who were to be shot to put their heads on a metal grate that drained into the Sava River, so that there would be minimal clean-up after the shootings. The accused and guards then ordered other detainees to move the bodies to one or two disposal areas where the bodies were piled until they were later loaded on trucks and taken to mass graves outside the town of Brcko or disposed of in other ways. 4) From about 21 May, 1992 until early July 1992, the detainees were subjected to beatings and, less frequently than before, killings. 5) In early July 1992, the surviving Luka detainees were transferred to another detention camp at Batkovic. 6) During the time Luka camp operated, the Serb authorities killed hundreds of Muslim and Croat detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 7) On about 1 May, 1992, Goran Jelisic, who was born on 7 June, 1968 in Bijeljina, came to Brcko from Bijeljina where he had worked as an agricultural machinery mechanic. During most of May 1992, Goran Jelisic held a position at Luka camp and called himself the "Serb Adolf."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just read the relevant paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 8) Ranko Cesic, who was born in 1964 in Drvar, lived in Brcko before the war. During May and June 1992, he acted under the apparent authority of the Brcko police and held a position of authority at Luka camp. General Allegations: 9) At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. 10) At all relevant times, Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic were required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949. 11) Goran Jelisic and Ranko Cesic are individually responsible for the crimes alleged against them in this indictment, pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Tribunal Statute. Individual criminal responsibility includes committing, planning, initiating, ordering, or aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of any crime referred to in Articles 2 to 5 of the Tribunal Statute. 12) All acts and omissions charged as crimes against humanity were part of a widespread, systematic or large-scale attack directed against the Muslim and Croat civilian population of Brcko. 13) Paragraphs 9 to 13 are re-alleged and incorporated into each of the charges set forth below. Charges: Count 1, genocide. 14) In May 1992, Goran Jelisic, intending to destroy a substantial or significant part of the Bosnian Muslim people as a national, ethnical, or religious group, systematically killed Muslim detainees at the Laser Bus Company, the Brcko police station, and Luka camp. He introduced himself as the "Serb Adolf," said that he had come to Brcko to kill Muslims, and often informed the Muslim detainees and others of the number of Muslims he had killed. In addition to killing countless detainees, whose identities are unknown, Goran Jelisic personally killed the victims described in paragraphs 16-25, 30, and 33. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed or aided and abetted: Count 1: Genocide, a crime recognized by Article 4(2)(a) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic, would you rise, please? Mr. Jelisic, do you hear me? Will you please rise? The first count has been read. This is the count of genocide. You heard it as it was read by the registrar. What I'm asking you is, as regards this count of genocide, which is recognised by Article 4(2)(a) of the Tribunal Statute, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, you plead not guilty. Mr. Babic, Mr. Londrovic, that is the meaning of the answer. Mr. Jelisic, you said that "I don't feel guilty." This is your opinion, if you like. What I'm asking you is whether procedurally you plead guilty or not guilty? Do you want your counsel to say that you are pleading not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are pleading not guilty; is that correct? Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Babic, let there be no ambiguity here. Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: No. There isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Jelisic. We will skip Counts 2 and 3, which refer to the co-accused, and move to Counts 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counts 4 and 5, killing of an unknown male. 16) On about 6 or 7 May, 1992, Goran Jelisic escorted an unknown male detainee down the street near the Brcko police station and then shot him in the head with a Scorpion pistol. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 4: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards this count, Count 4, Mr. Jelisic, you've heard it. Do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I understand Count 4, and I plead guilty to a violation of the laws or customs of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards Count 5, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 5: a crime against humanity recognized by Article 5(a) (murder) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty, Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am guilty of a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will move on to Counts 6 and 7.

By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 6: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead guilty to Count 6, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (murder) of the Geneva Conventions.

Goran Jelisic took Ahmet Hodzic to the same place where Goran Jelisic, earlier that day, had killed a young detainee from Sinteraj. After reaching the area, Goran Jelisic shot and killed Ahmet Hodzic. utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Counts 40 and 41, beatings of Amir Didic. 34) Between about 20 May and 28 May, 1992, at Luka camp, Goran Jelisic beat the Muslim detainee Amir Didic with a police baton causing Amir Didic to lose consciousness. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 40: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead guilty to Count 40, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) (cruel treatment) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 41: a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead guilty to Count 41, a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(i) (inhumane acts) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that we will not read Counts 42 and 43.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 44, plunder of private property. 36) From about 7 May to about 28 May, 1992, Goran Jelisic stole money belonging to persons detained at Luka camp, including Hasib Begic, Zejcir Osmic, Enes Zukic, and Armin Drapic. By these actions, Goran Jelisic committed: Count 44: a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3(e) (plunder) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty, Mr. Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I plead guilty to Count 44, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3(e) (plunder) of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Signed by the Deputy Prosecutor, Graham Blewitt, dated the 19th of October, 1998 at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jelisic. You may be seated. We must now speak about a certain number of methods that we are going to use in order to move forward. I would like to tell the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence that we find ourselves in a rather mixed situation. We have an accused who is pleading guilty to almost all of the counts, but pleads not guilty to Count 1, that is, the count of genocide. Let me remind you that as regards pleas of guilt, which concern almost all of the counts in the indictment, ordinarily, according to Rule 62 bis, and unless he is to retract his plea of not guilty, the Trial Chamber can now set the date for the sentencing hearing, but it must be ensured that the three conditions indicated in Rule 62 bis have been satisfied, that the guilty plea has been made voluntarily, that the guilty plea is not equivocal, and that there is sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation in it, either on the basis of independent indices or of a lack of any material disagreement between the parties about the facts of the case. As regards the application of the first condition, if the guilty plea was made voluntarily and is not equivocal, I suggest that in respect of what has just been said that, of course, we will record that the accused has pleaded guilty, and should he retract that, he should retract that as quickly as possible. As regards the third condition, let me say this, in light of the fact that, at the beginning of this hearing, the Defence counsel indicated a certain psychological condition. The counsel then retracted their request to postpone this hearing, but I would like to remind you that the plea of guilty must be made voluntarily and must not be equivocal. We know today that this was done, that it was done voluntarily, that it was not equivocal, but nonetheless, we are not going to set the sentencing hearing date today. I would like to be sure about the third condition, that is, that there is an agreement or that there is no material disagreement between the parties about the facts of the case about which Mr. Jelisic has pleaded guilty. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: With regard to the facts to which Goran Jelisic pleaded guilty, there is no disagreement between the Prosecution and the accused and his Defence lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic or Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what Mr. Tochilovsky said is exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you agree with your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. For a long time, the Prosecutors, the Defence counsel, and the accused have been working together, and the outcome of that is what the Honourable Trial Chamber has before it today. I am fully in agreement with what Mr. Tochilovsky and what Mr. Londrovic have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we now in a position to set a date for the sentencing hearing? A second possibility is, would you prefer that all this be related to the second aspect of our case, that is, the question of genocide and the fact that, to that count, Mr. Jelisic has pleaded not guilty and we're going to have a trial? As regards my second question, if you prefer that the possible sentence be handed down at the time of the final sentence regarding genocide, would you prefer that we postpone the date for that hearing? What is your opinion on that, Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before moving to this issue, there are two questions we would like the accused to clarify. We would like the accused to make it clear that the guilty plea wasn't affected by any threats, inducements, or promises. Secondly, we would like the accused to make it clear that he understands that the facts to which the accused admitted at this hearing will be used by the Prosecution, among other facts, in the trial on genocide. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic, you heard what Mr. Tochilovsky said. What is your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have understood, Your Honours, what Mr. Tochilovsky is proposing. As far as we are concerned, there are no problems whatsoever. Mr. Jelisic states that this is his voluntary statement, that nothing was promised to him, that he was not forced to enter such a plea. Mr. Jelisic is aware of the fact that the Prosecutor is going to use all of this for Count 1, genocide. However, the Defence shall do its best and hopes that it will convince this Honourable Court that Mr. Jelisic did not commit the crime of genocide. We shall attempt to do so during the trial. As far as the Defence is concerned, we propose that first we move to trial on Count 1, genocide, and then you hold a sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic, you have heard what was said. You understood what was said, that is, the fact that your plea of guilty has been recognised as valid by this Tribunal, and you must have a clear consciousness of what you are doing, what you are saying. Your counsel has explained to you what a crime against humanity is, what violations of the laws or customs of law are, and that you did not receive any threats, nor were given any promises. Do you feel today that you are in a position to say that that is the case, that you were not subjected to any pressure, that you were not given any promises, and that you're sure that those acts that you are saying that you are guilty of, that as part of the trial of genocide that will be held against you for which you pleaded not guilty, that these other facts can be used. Can you say to the Judges today that you are in that position, that is, that you made your guilty pleas voluntarily, non-equivocally, without pressure, without promises, and that this can be used against you as part of the trial for genocide. Can you answer these various questions? First of all, did you understand the sense of what I just asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could you please put your questions one at a time and could I answer them that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I hadn't quite understood the interpretation there. First of all, I wanted to ask you the question: When you plead guilty or not guilty, that you were not threatened, which would have forced you into making that plea of guilty, that there were no pressures, you were not subjected to any pressure or any kind of moral pressure? Do you understand what I'm asking you? Did somebody force you, as Judge Riad has just suggested that I express myself in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I understand you, Your Honour. No one promised me anything. No one threatened me. No one blackmailed me. It was my own goodwill that I admit the crime and save my soul, because there is no reason for me to keep this within myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did your counsel call your attention to the violations that -- not explaining it to you in a very broad manner, but did they explain to you what a crime against humanity, what violations of the laws or customs of war are? These are items which are somewhat indite, and this is why you have counsel. Did they explain to you what sentences you might be given, which could go as far as life imprisonment? Was this explained to you by your counsel? Did you understand what they explained to you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In contact with my lawyers, on several occasions, they explained this to me in detail and what the consequences of this may be. At any expense, I decided to admit these crimes, and I know that even life imprisonment may follow, but never mind. It is up to you to decide on my sentence after the trial, and I decided to admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Let me turn to your Defence counsel. Have you had the feeling, Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Babic, that you have called to the attention of your client all of the consequences that may arise from his plea?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Mr. Jelisic said, my distinguished colleague Mr. Babic and I, and as of late Mr. Kostic as well, who, due to illness, is not here today, we have explained to Mr. Jelisic the essence of what a crime against humanity is and what a war crime is. We explained to him the gravity of these crimes. We told him about the sentences. We also told him what all the rights are that he is waiving on the basis of the Statute and the Rules when he pleads guilty. Professionally, we even advised him not to plead guilty to a crime against humanity. However, Mr. Jelisic decided to reveal his soul, as he said himself to this Honourable Trial Chamber, to simply cleanse his soul and to sincerely repent for what he has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now turn to the Office of the Prosecutor. We now find ourselves in the situation in which the questions you asked were answered clearly. Do you feel that you were given clear answers to the questions that you were asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to consult with my colleagues. The Judges have deliberated, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 62 bis, and have noted that the guilty plea was made voluntarily, that it was not equivocal, and that it was done in full knowledge of the facts, and that the elements provided by the Office of the Prosecutor in support of this hearing are sufficient to establish the crime and the accused's participation in it, either on the basis of these elements and/or the fact that there was no fundamental disagreement between the parties as regards all of the facts of this case for which Goran Jelisic decided to plead guilty. Nonetheless, the Judges feel that concerning the fact that there is one count, that is, Count 1, genocide, to which the accused did not plead guilty, the Judges consider that they will declare that the accused is guilty on all the other counts after the trial on genocide. Let my explain myself. The Judges consider that condition 1 of Rule 62 bis has been satisfied, as has 2 and that 3 has been satisfied. The Judges could state that the accused is guilty today, but since there will be a trial for genocide, before pronouncing a single sentence, the Judges will make that statement at the end of the trial for genocide. In any case, for that case, there must be a trial which will allow us to move to a final sentencing decision, not only in respect of the conduct of the trial on genocide, but on all of the elements, including the guilty pleas of Goran Jelisic, which were made in the trial for genocide. Is that clear? Defence counsel? Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, Mr. Londrovic? All right. Mr. Jelisic, have you understood the Trial Chamber's position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. I have understood, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me remind you that there is a Pre-Trial Judge who, in this case, is Judge Riad. If you agree, we will suspend the hearing today, and I invite Judge Riad, at a date that Mr. Fourmy will set with the judge, a date for a Status Conference so that we can know when we can move, first of all, into the genocide trial, and then the handing down of the sentence once the Trial Chamber has declared the accused guilty of the crimes to which he pleaded guilty. The Court stands adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: Pages 216 to 234 - redacted – in private session.
